passage_flags: Mild: the argument closely tracks the real 2021 #TranslatorsOnTheCover campaign and Jennifer Croft's Guardian essay on naming translators on covers (down to the 'invisible translator' framing and the prize/press-release complaint). [1] is no concession; [2] overstates into an attack on the jury's qualifications the paragraph never makes; [3] generalizes to an industry trend the passage never asserts.

The example immediately follows and illustrates the claim that a sentence is a set of choices a second language can only answer, and the paragraph ends with 'the English reader would believe the author had chosen it.' Other options pull claims from ¶4 and ¶5 that the example does not directly support.

'Partly... Partly... And partly' enumerates three causes; 'The effect is circular' names the loop. No classification of translators [1], no contrast yielding opposite remedies [2], no narration of personal dealings with publishers [3].

The rhetorical question 'Did any of those four thousand correspondents imagine that a person, rather than a department, was reading them' asks readers to look at how they themselves behave. Option 0 contradicts the writer's sympathy for maintainers. Option 1 builds a comparison from one example. Option 2 is wrong because she never challenges the survey.

The sentence comes right after 'I will grant that money has saved projects' and backs up that concession. The hours-versus-dollars claim appears only in paragraph 5. Nothing in the passage supports options 2 or 3.

Paragraph 2 calls the diagnosis 'a good one,' and paragraph 3 says the book 'loses its footing' when it turns to the cure. The writer's own solution comes in paragraph 5, not paragraph 3, so option 1 fails. Paragraph 3 attacks the remedy, not the survey's findings, so option 3 fails.

The sentence connects the personal story back to the review by praising Alcock's empathy while calling his sponsorship remedy puzzling. The tone is admiring, not contemptuous, so option 0 fails. The sentence does not say the second half is redeemed, so option 2 fails. The proposal itself is introduced in paragraph 5, so option 3 fails.
